table.title: Mathematical Notation Reference
table.html:
SymbolNameLaTeXMeaning
∑Summation\sumDenotes the sum of a sequence of terms; an index and lower and upper bounds are usually written below and above the sign, as in ∑i=1n ai.
∫Integral\intRepresents an integral, used for antiderivatives and for definite integrals that accumulate a quantity over an interval or region; limits of integration may be attached to the sign.
∇Nabla\nablaA vector differential operator that produces the gradient of a scalar field and, depending on how it is combined with a vector field, the divergence or curl.
⊗Tensor product\otimesDenotes the tensor product of vector spaces or modules, or the Kronecker product of matrices; the intended construction is usually indicated by the surrounding context.
ℵ₀Aleph-null\aleph_0The cardinality of countably infinite sets such as the natural numbers; it is the smallest infinite cardinal number in standard set theory.
table.brief: Math notation table: Symbol (∑, ∫, ∇, ⊗, ℵ₀) / Name / LaTeX (like \otimes) / Meaning (long)

understanding.purpose: A reference for identifying mathematical symbols, their names, LaTeX commands, and meanings.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the symbol or name, then compare the corresponding command and explanation across the row. Explanations are much longer than the other entries and will determine most row heights.
groups: Symbol and Name identify the same notation in visual and verbal form.
LaTeX gives the input command for the notation; Meaning explains its use.
keep_intact: Symbols and LaTeX commands, including backslashes and subscripts.
Names and column headers where space permits.
may_wrap: Meaning can wrap at word boundaries; its length gives other cells room to wrap within the same row.
Multiword names can wrap between words.

preferred.name: r2C
preferred.note: Try a middle ground between r1A and r1B: allow 60px of overflow while giving Meaning more room than r1B, preserving intact words and commands.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Give Meaning 124px of text width, enough for its longest unbreakable word, while keeping the other lookup keys intact. The 399px table limits horizontal scrolling to 40px.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Use the minimum stated widths that preserve all unbreakable entries. The 375px table extends 16px beyond the width limit, testing whether a small scroll can avoid the word and command splits seen in the viewport-fitting designs.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Refine r1A by giving Meaning 30px more. This costs additional horizontal scrolling but should improve sentence rhythm and reduce row heights while preserving intact identifiers.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Increase Meaning from r2C to 190px to reduce line count while keeping horizontal overflow below r2A.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Give Meaning the minimum width needed for its longest word, preserving intact text with only 16px of horizontal overflow.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Widen Name to keep Tensor product on one line and give Meaning a readable measure; compare the cleaner identification columns against the added horizontal scrolling.

bad.name: r2B
bad.note: Fit the table within 359px by narrowing Meaning to 105px. This tests whether eliminating horizontal scrolling is worth the resulting word splits and longer rows.
bad.why: The narrow Meaning column splits words and produces very tall rows, making the explanations difficult to read and separating each symbol from the next.

rationale: r2C keeps symbols, names and LaTeX commands intact while giving the explanatory prose enough width to read in reasonably sized phrases. The Tensor product name wraps naturally, preserving space for Meaning. The table extends 60px beyond the viewport, so readers must scroll sideways to see complete lines, but the rows are substantially less elongated than in the narrower alternatives.

general: Protect identifiers and unbreakable words before allocating the remaining width to prose.
Judge horizontal scrolling against the readability and row height gained by wider columns.
A multiword label can wrap naturally when that frees useful space for longer content.
specific: The Meaning column drives row height because its entries are much longer than the other columns.
Widening Name to keep Tensor product on one line moves more of Meaning outside the initial viewport.

tradeoffs: r1B asks for less horizontal scrolling but makes the prose noticeably narrower and the rows taller. r3A and r2A make the explanations more comfortable after scrolling, at the cost of hiding more of each line initially.
uncertain: The preferred balance depends on how readily readers discover and use horizontal scrolling. The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not browser-tested guarantees of identical wrapping; they assume the other columns remain near the preferred proportions.

critique.good: The full table fits the viewport. Headers, symbols, names, and LaTeX commands remain readable, and the identifier columns are easy to scan.
critique.problems: The meanings form narrow, tall text columns, making rows difficult to read across and leaving large empty areas in the identifier columns. Words such as “antiderivatives” and “construction” split mid-word.
critique.cause: Meaning has only 84px of text width at a 105px column width, less than its longest unbreakable word requires.

critique.good: Names and commands stay intact, while the wider meanings read in more coherent phrases. Shorter rows make the relationship between each symbol and its explanation easier to follow.
critique.problems: The viewport cuts through every meaning, so reading an explanation requires horizontal scrolling. The single-line name column consumes space that could be given to meaning or returned to the viewport.
critique.cause: The 462px table exceeds the width limit by 103px; the 126px Name column keeps “Tensor product” on one line but pushes Meaning farther right.

critique.good: The full table fits, and the wider Meaning column improves the prose rhythm and reduces row height compared with r0A.
critique.problems: “Summation” and the LaTeX command “\aleph_0” split, damaging two important lookup keys. The meanings remain narrow and the rows still contain substantial vertical whitespace.
critique.cause: Name has only 64px of text width at 85px, and LaTeX has only 51px at 72px; both are narrower than their longest unbreakable entries.

critique.good: The identification columns and commands remain intact, and the wider Meaning column gives explanations a more readable rhythm and keeps rows comparatively short. Tensor product wraps naturally between words.
critique.problems: The viewport cuts through the explanations, so readers must scroll sideways to read them in full. Tall explanation cells also leave substantial blank space in the first three columns.
critique.cause: The 180px Meaning column brings the table to 435px, 75px beyond the viewport; the long explanations still govern row height.

critique.good: Headers, names and commands remain intact, and the overflow is smaller than in r1A.
critique.problems: The viewport still cuts through Meaning, while its narrow lines make explanations noticeably choppy and stretch the rows. The large blank areas weaken the sense of each row as a unit.
critique.cause: Reducing Meaning to 145px saves 35px of scrolling but increases wrapping substantially; the first three columns retain the same widths.

critique.good: Only 16px lies beyond the viewport, and words, names and commands remain intact.
critique.problems: The explanations form very narrow, fragmented text blocks, making the table exceptionally tall and leaving the identifying columns mostly empty. Even with this compromise, the right edge still requires scrolling.
critique.cause: Meaning has only 100px of text space at 121px total width, just enough for its longest unbreakable word.

critique.good: Symbols, names, commands and headers remain intact; the wider Meaning column gives explanations a readable measure and keeps related cells together in moderately tall rows.
critique.problems: Much of each explanation lies beyond the initial viewport, requiring horizontal scrolling. The Tensor product name wraps, while the identifier columns contain substantial empty space below their entries.
critique.cause: The 210px Meaning column brings the total width to 464px, about 105px beyond the available width; the 99px Name column cannot hold Tensor product on one line.

critique.good: All four columns fit at first sight, and the symbols, names, commands and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The explanations form narrow, long stacks, with mid-word splits and very tall rows. This makes comparing entries vertically laborious and leaves large empty areas in the first three columns.
critique.cause: At 105px, Meaning has only 84px of text space, less than its 100px longest unbreakable word.

critique.good: All headers and commands remain intact, explanations wrap without splitting words, and the scroll distance is smaller than in r2A.
critique.problems: The initial viewport still shows only the beginning of Meaning, while the narrower explanations make rows considerably taller than in r2A. Tensor product wraps across two lines.
critique.cause: The 165px Meaning column leaves only about 106px of that column visible initially, and its 144px text measure creates more lines than r2A. The 99px Name column wraps the longest multiword name.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r2B.why: All columns fit in the viewport and the symbols, names and LaTeX are easy to scan. The narrow Meaning column creates very tall rows and splits words such as ‘antiderivatives’ and ‘construction’.

r1B.why: The identifying columns stay readable and the wider Meaning column keeps words intact with less wrapping. Reading the descriptions requires horizontal scrolling.

r2C.why: The wider Meaning column gives the prose a more comfortable measure, but more of each description lies beyond the viewport, increasing the cost of comparing it with the symbol and name.

ref_equal.why: Equal-looking narrow columns waste space on short symbols while splitting names and many words in the descriptions. The resulting tall rows are difficult to read.

r1C.why: The identifiers remain intact and the descriptions wrap without the conspicuous word splits seen in A. A small amount of horizontal scrolling is needed to see the ends of some lines.

ref_auto.why: The identifiers stay intact and the Meaning column keeps words together. Only a small part of the table extends beyond the viewport, although some line endings still require scrolling.

raw.unsure: E and F appear nearly identical, so their small difference is hard to judge. The supplied images do not make the full horizontal extent of B and C clear, which limits comparison of their scrolling cost.

ref_equal.why: Equal-width columns leave Meaning extremely narrow, splitting many words and making the rows very tall; even Summation breaks.

r2B.why: The table fits the viewport and keeps the names and LaTeX commands readable, but Meaning is still narrow enough to split words such as antiderivatives and construction.

r1B.why: The wider Meaning column preserves words and gives the descriptions a more natural rhythm, while names and commands remain intact. Reading the ends of lines requires horizontal scrolling.

r1C.why: Names and commands stay intact, and the descriptions wrap without the conspicuous word splits seen in B. A small amount of Meaning extends beyond the viewport.

ref_auto.why: The first three columns remain clear, and Meaning has enough width to preserve words with only a small horizontal overflow. Its narrow prose measure still makes rows fairly tall.

r2C.why: The wider prose column improves line length and reduces row height, but a substantial part of each description lies beyond the initial viewport, increasing the need to scroll.

raw.unsure: D and E appear almost identical; any small difference in overflow is difficult to judge from the images. The full right edges of C and F are not visible in the supplied display, so their exact scrolling cost is uncertain.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
